title: The tale on the quays of Cuan shean
summary: In the moon of Faolach the word of a far coast is on the quay at Cuan shean, told in the lee of the rope-sheds and at the crews' fire. No one says he saw the coast, and every telling leads back to another. By the moon's end it is told at Ros bheag, Inis àrsaidh and Ceann mhòr.

title: The pilot of Ros bheag
summary: A pilot of Ros bheag, blown off the land in the autumn gales, comes home after nine days with his water gone. The coast shows up in the talk as his, but he swears he saw nothing but grey water, too loudly.

title: The Cuan shean crew heard in the red hall
summary: Eachann mac Lachlainn, skipper of Cuan shean, tells the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west, with smoke on it and no hall. Asked if he was first to hear it, he says he was about the last.

title: The Ros bheag crew heard in the red hall
summary: Oighrig nic Raghnaill, skipper of Ros bheag, tells the queen that the coast lies north past the north cape, high and forested, with a white river, and that the pilot who saw it swore on the cup at Seann Skell.

title: The Ceann mhòr crew heard in the red hall
summary: Tòmas mac Uilleim of Ceann mhòr tells the queen that the land lies east behind the mist, and can be smelt on some mornings; the old men of the north-west have always said so.

title: Murchadh's leaf of the three tellings
summary: The queen's scribe Murchadh mac Eòghainn writes the three tellings on one leaf and adds at its foot that they agree on the coast and on nothing else. The leaf is kept in the chest of the red hall.

title: How many days' water
summary: At the lower board of the red hall the queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill asks the Cuan shean skipper how many days' water a boat would need. He answers that no boat of the island could make the crossing, and that none has ever been built that could.

title: The question at the hearths
summary: Through the moon of Dubhlas the question 'Would we go?' is asked at hearths from Baile chrom to Seann Vell, most of all on the west coast. No lots are drawn and no lord or priest gives a word.

title: Two households of Inis àrsaidh
summary: In the drying-shed at Inis àrsaidh two households say before the whole town that they will go if a boat is ever made that can make the crossing. The town laughs, then stops laughing.

title: A custodian asks for the three tellings
summary: Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a young custodian of the western diggings, comes down to Cathair dhearg on an errand of the vein-house and asks to hear the three tellings from the queen's scribe.

title: Mòrag at Cuan shean
summary: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides alone to Cuan shean and questions Eachann mac Lachlainn on seams, winds and wood. He tells her a hull that needs no sewing would want great oak and a keel, and that no one alive knows how to set one.

title: The queen keeps the journey from the roll
summary: Queen Beathag watches her sister walk the Cuan shean skipper to the gate of the red hall and look down the river road west. She bids Murchadh write nothing of it, since it is no matter for the roll yet.

title: The ninth year of Queen Beathag
summary: The red hall's rolls enter the first year of the age as the ninth year of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, crowned at fifteen and now three-and-twenty: a good year for barley and a middling one for fish, with no child yet born to her.

title: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill at nineteen
summary: The queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, nineteen years old and two years married to a man of the western shore she chose herself, comes up to the capital for the winter and sits at the lower board when the crews are heard.
